name: American Red Cross: blood supply and lifesaving training (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US blood supply and US training courses.
summary: The American Red Cross collects about 40% of the US blood supply (6.4 million blood products to some 2,500 hospitals in its fiscal year to June 2025, the latest audited year: the FY2026 accounts weren't on the Red Cross's financials page on 4 November 2026) and trains about 6 million people a year in CPR, first aid and water safety. Hospitals and course fees pay for both, and more than their cost (biomedical revenue $2.31 billion against $2.12 billion of expenses; programme-materials (mainly course) revenue $175 million against $143 million), so this model has weight 0 in what a donation to the Red Cross does; it shows what the work itself achieves per dollar spent on it, in years of healthy life per $1,000. Both branches are discounted for missing data: the deaths averted per blood product rest on judgments anchored on studies of patients who refused transfusion, and the training on registry studies of bystander CPR. The biggest uncertainty is the counterfactual: other US blood centres and course providers would supply most of it if the Red Cross didn't. The result is far below the site's global-health median because other providers would step in (only 15% of the outcome counted), the Red Cross's product is under a quarter of the resources behind each transfusion, both branches take the missing-data step, and a transfusion survivor lives about three-fifths of an average remaining life. Together the adjustments leave about 1% of the raw outcome; before them a death averted costs about $25,000 of blood, several times what one costs in the site's global-health programmes; it is mostly uncertainty (the judgments behind deaths averted per product span a wide range).

sections.title: Cost

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

Blood products supplied to hospitals, FY2025

source.title: American Red Cross, Annual Report, Fiscal Year 2025 (July 2024 - June 2025)
source.quote: 6.4 million blood products provided to help patients.

rows.explainer: Red cells, platelets, plasma and cryoprecipitate; the blood chain below counts per product, not per patient (a patient often gets several).

rows.label: Cost per blood product (all programmes' cost here, for context)
rows.explainer: Context only: the cost here includes training.

rows.label: Years a product's effect is counted
rows.explainer: A transfusion's effect on survival is immediate and counted once.

rows.label: Share of blood products given to acutely bleeding patients
rows.explainer: Trauma, obstetric, surgical and gastrointestinal haemorrhage; the rest goes to chronic anaemia (cancer, blood disorders, kidney disease) and prophylactic platelets. Anchor: US and UK audits of red-cell use put surgery and trauma at about a third to a half of units and medical (chronic) use at the rest.

rows.label: Risk an acutely bleeding transfused patient would die with no blood available
rows.explainer: Anchor: patients who refuse transfusion (Jehovah's Witnesses) and are left with very low haemoglobin after surgery die much more often: in Carson et al. (2002, Transfusion 42:812-8), 30-day mortality rose steeply as postoperative haemoglobin fell below about 5 g/dL, to roughly a third of patients and more at the lowest levels. Acutely bleeding transfused patients range from those who would have coped (most) to massive haemorrhage; we take 15% dying without any blood, from 5% to 30%.

rows.label: Risk of death without blood, per product's recipient
rows.explainer: Acutely bleeding share × their risk of dying with no blood (acute deaths only; transfusion-dependent patients' deaths are added in deaths_averted_per_person).

rows.label: Blood products per acutely bleeding patient
rows.explainer: Deaths per product are the mean risk over the mean products per acutely bleeding patient, red cells, plasma and platelets together. Most acute transfusions are 2-4 units, with a tail of massive transfusions (10 or more units in 24 hours) that raises the mean: about 4.5, from 3 to 8. A judgment; no US survey of components per acutely bleeding patient was found.

rows.label: Share of that risk one product removes
rows.explainer: Each product's share of the patient's survival.

rows.label: Acute-bleeding deaths averted per product (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Risk without blood × each product's share of a patient's survival.

rows.label: Deaths caused indirectly, per direct death averted (none)
rows.explainer: 0: the deaths counted are all the transfusion's own.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Deaths averted per product: acutely bleeding recipients (risk × each product's share × years) plus transfusion-dependent chronic patients (bld_chronic_deaths_per_product). Both are valued at the blood recipients' age mix: haematology-oncology patients are about as old as other recipients.

rows.label: Share of deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Neonatal and paediatric transfusion is a small share of US blood use; most recipients are adults, half over 65.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Of recipients over five, children 5-14 are about 2% (paediatric oncology and trauma): US transfusion is overwhelmingly adult. Low end if paediatric use is even rarer, high end if paediatric hospitals' share is larger.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Trauma and obstetric bleeding are younger; surgical and medical recipients are mostly over 50, valued by their own ages below.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the mortality and income benefits
rows.explainer: 0: illness is counted once, in DALYs (dalys_illness_averted_per_person).

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: obstetric haemorrhage deaths are counted as maternal deaths above.

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, ln(consumption) per year
rows.explainer: 0: no income effect is modelled for transfusion or training.

rows.label: Years until the income gain starts
rows.explainer: Not used: there is no income gain.

rows.label: Years the long-term income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a long-term income gain lasts (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, present value
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included, so the result moves with it. Never type in a present value worked out elsewhere: rebuild it from its inputs.

rows.label: Resource sharing within households (multiplier on an earner's gain)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's): an earner's income gain is shared with the household, so it counts this many times. Read by every model that values a long-term income gain (INV-13).

rows.label: Blood: internal validity of the blood chain
rows.explainer: No trial withholds blood; the chain is built from audit shares and judgments about survival without transfusion. Anchor: the site's observational health effects at 0.5-0.8.

rows.label: Blood: external validity: the trials' setting against this program's, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The judgments above are already made for US hospitals today, so no transfer from another setting is needed (1); the low end allows for the shares being taken from audits older than today's restrictive transfusion practice.

rows.label: Blood: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The product of its two parts.

rows.label: Blood: share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: If the Red Cross didn't collect, hospitals would buy from the other US blood centres (America's Blood Centers members and Vitalant supply the other 60%), which have expanded before when big suppliers changed. But the system runs with only a few days' stock: national shortage declarations (the Red Cross's January 2022 'national blood crisis', the 2024 emergency shortage) show that supply lost is not replaced at once, and hospitals then postpone surgery. What is lost without the Red Cross is mostly the transition (a year or two of a 40% gap filling) and a thinner reserve for disasters. About 0.15 of its product's value, from 0.05 (others replace it within months) to 0.4 (lasting shortfall).

rows.label: Blood: this charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: The Red Cross's full cost (overhead included, as in cost_total) against all the resources behind the transfusions: its own cost, the hospitals' costs of transfusing beyond the purchase price, and the donors' time at the US value of an hour: about a quarter.
rows.formula: bio_spend * overhead_ratio / (bio_spend * overhead_ratio + (bld_abc_cost_multiple - 1) * bio_revenue + bld_donations * bld_hours_per_donation * trn_hour_value)

rows.label: Full cost of transfusing a unit, as a multiple of its purchase price

source.title: Shander et al. (2010), Activity-based costs of blood transfusions in surgical patients at four hospitals, Transfusion 50:753-65 (abstract)
source.quote: 3.2- to 4.8-fold higher than blood product acquisition costs

rows.explainer: Activity-based costing at four hospitals: testing, storage, administration and monitoring make the full cost several times the purchase price. Midpoint 4.

rows.label: Blood and platelet donations collected, FY2025

source.title: American Red Cross, Annual Report, Fiscal Year 2025 (July 2024 - June 2025)
source.quote: MORE THAN 4.6 million blood donations and 1.1 million platelet donations collected.

rows.explainer: 4.6 million blood plus 1.1 million platelet donations.

rows.label: Donor's hours per donation, travel included
rows.explainer: Whole blood takes about an hour at the drive plus travel (about 1.5 hours); platelet apheresis two to three hours plus travel (about 3.3). Weighted by 4.6 and 1.1 million donations: about 1.8, from 1.3 to 2.5.

rows.label: Blood: delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: Products distributed that expire unused in hospitals (a few per cent of red cells, more for platelets).

rows.label: Blood: leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Hospitals pay for the products; no donor money is funged here.

rows.label: Years a donation waits before the charity spends it
rows.explainer: Blood is collected and used within weeks; there are no donations waiting to be spent.

rows.label: Blood: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: the products are the Red Cross's own count, but the deaths averted per product rest on judgments (the share given for acute bleeding, the risk of dying without blood, products per patient) anchored on studies of patients who refused transfusion, not on a measurement of what the Red Cross's supply changes. So the shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Years from the charity's spending to the intervention reaching people
rows.explainer: Red cells keep 42 days, platelets 5-7: the delay to use is weeks.

rows.label: Years from delivery to the middle of the protection
rows.explainer: 0: the benefit comes at the transfusion.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the benefits come
rows.explainer: Every wait is discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit (the income gain's own wait is counted from delivery, in ln_income_gain_per_person).

rows.label: Blood: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: bld_evidence_adj * bld_counterfactual_adj * bld_attribution_share * bld_implementation_adj * bld_leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * bld_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above, the missing-data step included.

rows.label: Treatment costs averted, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: 0: transfusion is itself the treatment; it doesn't avert later treatment costs on this model's scale.

rows.label: Rebound malaria from lost immunity, as a share of value lost
rows.explainer: 0: no immunity effect.

rows.label: Investment of income increases, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: 0: no income gain.

rows.label: Other benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Health screening for donors (the Red Cross notifies donors with high blood pressure and other findings) (+), the national disaster reserve (+), drownings averted by water safety and first aid beyond CPR (+); transfusion reactions and infections (−, very rare) and CPR survivors left with brain injury (−).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: GiveWell-style supplementary adjustments, each its own row, summed: they add to the modelled value as one share, as in GiveWell's sheets.

rows.label: People trained in lifesaving skills, FY2025

source.title: American Red Cross, Annual Report, Fiscal Year 2025 (July 2024 - June 2025)
source.page: p. 2, letter from the chair and CEO
source.quote: Last year our humanitarian organization also trained more than 6 million people in critical skills such as first aid, water safety, CPR and AED usage

rows.explainer: People who completed a course (the '25 million reached' on p. 14 includes online and app users).

rows.label: Share of trainees taught CPR
rows.explainer: First Aid/CPR/AED and Basic Life Support are the core courses; water safety and lifeguarding trained only 'more than 30,000' of the 6 million (annual report p. 14), and babysitting and other courses are a minority. About 85%, from 70 to 95%.

rows.label: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in the US per year

source.title: American Heart Association, CPR Facts and Stats
source.quote: More than 350,000 cardiac arrests occur outside of the hospital each year.

rows.explainer: EMS-assessed non-traumatic arrests; the low end is the newer count of those EMS treats (over 250,000). (The AHA page blocks automated fetches; the same figure is in the AHA's Heart Disease and Stroke Statistics updates.)

rows.label: US population, 2024
rows.explainer: The site's US population (World Bank), to turn arrests into a yearly chance per person of being there when one happens.

rows.label: People present who could start CPR, per arrest
rows.explainer: Three in four arrests happen at home, usually with one or two family members present; public arrests have more bystanders.

rows.label: Extra chance a trained bystander gives CPR
rows.explainer: About 40% of US arrests get bystander CPR (CARES); people trained in the past two years are much more willing and able to start, but many trained bystanders are not the one who acts. Population studies of training: in Denmark, each 5-point rise in the share of people taking a course went with 14% higher odds of survival, about 40% of it through more bystander CPR (Jensen et al. 2023, JAMA Network Open 6:e233338); a year-long US county training drive raised bystander CPR by 3 points overall (not significant) and 9 points in public places, with no significant change in survival to discharge (Toy et al. 2026, Resuscitation); a meta-analysis of 19 observational studies finds layperson training associated with higher survival to discharge (CPR training odds ratio 1.74, 1.39-2.19: Pan et al. 2026, Frontiers in Public Health). Those are population averages over everyone; for a trained person who is present, a rise of about 25 points, from 10 to 40.

rows.label: Extra survival when a bystander gives CPR

source.title: Hasselqvist-Ax et al. (2015), Early cardiopulmonary resuscitation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, N Engl J Med 372:2307-15 (abstract)
source.quote: The 30-day survival rate was 10.5% when CPR was performed before EMS arrival versus 4.0% when CPR was not performed before EMS arrival (P<0.001).

rows.explainer: In 30,381 witnessed arrests in Sweden, 30-day survival was 4.0% without CPR before the ambulance; the adjusted odds ratio 2.15 (1.88-2.45) on 4.0% gives 8.2% (7.3-9.3%), a gain of 4.2 points (3.6-4.8). A trained bystander who is present is close to the witnessed case. Observational, adjusted for known confounders (the evidence adjustment carries the rest).

rows.label: Years a trainee's skills count
rows.explainer: Certification lasts two years; skills fade within one to two years without practice.

rows.label: Cardiac-arrest deaths averted by a year's trainees (before adjustments)
rows.formula: trn_people_trained * trn_cpr_share * trn_ohca_per_year * trn_bystanders_per_arrest / trn_us_population * trn_extra_cpr_prob * trn_survival_gain * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, trn_skill_years)
rows.explainer: Trainees × CPR share × yearly chance of being at an arrest × extra chance of acting × extra survival × discounted years. About 160, against the 230 lives the Red Cross credited to its trainees in FY2025 (annual report p. 15, its lifesaving awards, many of whom would have been saved anyway).

rows.label: Training: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The survival effect is observational, survivors are sometimes left with brain damage, and the chain's middle steps are judgments. Anchor: the blood chain's 0.75, lower for more steps.

rows.label: Training: share of trainees who wouldn't have been trained elsewhere
rows.explainer: Most trainees take the course because their job requires certification (health care, schools, lifeguards, workplaces) and would take the American Heart Association's or another provider's course instead.

rows.label: Hours a trainee spends on the course
rows.explainer: Blended First Aid/CPR/AED courses take about 2-5 hours, Basic Life Support about 3-4, lifeguarding much longer.

rows.label: Value of an hour of a trainee's time (US$)
rows.explainer: The site's US value of an hour of unpaid time, 2024 (@united_states.volunteer_hour_value_2024, Independent Sector: the BLS wage plus fringe benefits), as for the Red Cross's volunteers in the disaster model; also prices the blood donors' time.

rows.label: Training: the Red Cross's share of the resources behind it
rows.formula: trn_spend * overhead_ratio / (trn_spend * overhead_ratio + trn_people_trained * trn_course_hours * trn_hour_value)
rows.explainer: Course costs (overhead included) against the trainees' (or their employers') own hours on the course, which are most of the resources: about 0.15. Licensed partner instructors teaching Red Cross courses are counted at zero (their cost isn't published), so this errs high.

rows.label: Training: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Trainees counted who didn't finish the hands-on part, or blended learners who never booked the skills session.

rows.label: Training: leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Course fees pay for the training, so no donor money is funged (1); the ends allow for employers shifting course spending between providers (below) or Red Cross courses drawing in workplace programmes that would not otherwise run (above).

rows.label: Training: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: trainees are the Red Cross's own count, but whether they are at an arrest and act because of the course are judgments, and the survival effect comes from registry studies of bystander CPR in general (Hasselqvist-Ax et al. 2015), not an evaluation of Red Cross trainees. So the shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Blood: deaths averted before adjustments (weights only)
rows.explainer: Weights the canonical rows below.

rows.label: Blood's share of the deaths averted before adjustments
rows.explainer: Weights the canonical adjustment rows, which are for reading only.

rows.label: Training: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: trn_evidence_adj * trn_counterfactual_adj * trn_attribution_share * trn_implementation_adj * trn_leverage_funging_adj * trn_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The training branch's own adjustments, the missing-data step included; its effect is immediate (no wait).

rows.label: Internal validity (branch average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: This is the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row; training's evidence adjustment stands for its internal validity.

rows.label: External validity (branch average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: This is the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row; training's judgments are already for the US, so 1.

rows.label: Evidence adj (branch average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: This is the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Counterfactual adj (branch average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: This is the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Attribution share shared (branch average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: This is the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The canonical share of credit, the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Implementation adj (branch average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: This is the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Leverage funging adj (branch average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: This is the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Missing-data step (branch average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: This is the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row, and both are thin.

rows.label: Total adj (branch average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: This is the outcome-weighted average of the branches (blood and training, weighted by deaths averted before adjustments), for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Training: cardiac-arrest deaths averted, after adjustments
Training: share of the arrests averted at ages 15-49
rows.explainer: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is mostly a disease of older adults; children are under 2% and counted here as 15-49.

rows.label: Training: value of a cardiac-arrest death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Cardiac-arrest victims are mostly over 50, valued by five-year weights; drownings averted by water safety are younger and in unmodelled benefits.

rows.label: Training: a cardiac-arrest survivor's remaining life as a share of an average person's of the same age
rows.explainer: Survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest discharged alive have heart disease and some excess long-term mortality against their age peers, though most live for years: about 0.8, from 0.65 to 0.95, the same step as the blood survivors' (a judgment: no study of US survivors' remaining life against age peers was read).

rows.label: Blood: deaths averted (after adjustments)
Blood: of the deaths averted at 50 or older, share aged 50 to 64
rows.explainer: Transfusion recipients are old: in US surveys of blood use about half of red cells go to patients 65 and over, a third of them 75+. Of recipients over 50, about 30% are 50-64, 30% 65-74 and 40% 75+; acute bleeding (trauma, obstetrics) is younger, which the 15-49 share carries.

rows.label: Blood: of the deaths averted at 50 or older, share aged 65 to 74
rows.explainer: The same anchor; the rest are 75 or older. The range runs from an older to a younger mix.

rows.label: Blood: a survivor's remaining life as a share of an average person's of the same age
rows.explainer: Transfusion recipients are sicker than their age peers and die sooner: in 1.1 million Scandinavian recipients, survival was 73.7% at one year, 53.4% at five and 27.0% at twenty, with mortality still 1.3 times the general population's after 17 years (Kamper-Jørgensen et al. 2008, Transfusion 48:2577-84, PMID 18673342). Applied to the acute-bleeding deaths; transfusion-dependent patients take their own share (bld_dependent_survivor_life_share). The value of a death averted assumes an average remaining life for the age, so a blood survivor's counts at a share of it. Acute-bleeding survivors (trauma, obstetric, surgical) do better than the all-recipient cohort, whose internal-medicine patients do worst: about 0.65, from 0.45 to 0.85.

rows.label: Blood: a transfusion-dependent survivor's remaining life as a share of an average person's of the same age
rows.explainer: Haematology-oncology patients do worst among transfusion recipients (in Kamper-Jørgensen et al. 2008, survival was lowest for those transfused in internal medicine), and five-year survival after acute leukaemia, myelodysplasia or transplant is well under half: about 0.4, from 0.25 to 0.6.

rows.label: Blood: value of a death averted at 50 or older (units of value)
rows.formula: bld_share_50_64_of_50plus * avg(@moral_weights.givewell_age_50_54, @moral_weights.givewell_age_55_59, @moral_weights.givewell_age_60_64) + bld_share_65_74_of_50plus * avg(@moral_weights.givewell_age_65_69, @moral_weights.givewell_age_70_74) + (1 - bld_share_50_64_of_50plus - bld_share_65_74_of_50plus) * avg(@moral_weights.givewell_age_75_79, @moral_weights.givewell_age_80_84, @moral_weights.givewell_age_85_plus)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year moral weights mixed by the deaths' ages, as rich-country care requires (families/high-income-care.md), instead of the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Training: of the deaths averted at 50 or older, share aged 50 to 64
rows.explainer: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest's median age is about 62 (CARES): of arrests over 50, about 45% are 50-64, 30% 65-74 and 25% 75+, the oldest less often in public places where trained bystanders are.

rows.label: Training: of the deaths averted at 50 or older, share aged 65 to 74
rows.explainer: The same anchor; the rest are 75 or older. The range runs from an older to a younger mix.

rows.label: Training: value of a death averted at 50 or older (units of value)
rows.formula: trn_share_50_64_of_50plus * avg(@moral_weights.givewell_age_50_54, @moral_weights.givewell_age_55_59, @moral_weights.givewell_age_60_64) + trn_share_65_74_of_50plus * avg(@moral_weights.givewell_age_65_69, @moral_weights.givewell_age_70_74) + (1 - trn_share_50_64_of_50plus - trn_share_65_74_of_50plus) * avg(@moral_weights.givewell_age_75_79, @moral_weights.givewell_age_80_84, @moral_weights.givewell_age_85_plus)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year moral weights mixed by the deaths' ages, as rich-country care requires (families/high-income-care.md), instead of the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Blood: value of a death averted at the recipients' age mix (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band (the over-50s by five-year weights), times your value of a life.

rows.label: Deaths averted (blood and training, after adjustments)
rows.explainer: Both branches' deaths averted.

rows.label: Value of a death averted, both branches (units of value)
rows.formula: (people_reached * bld_total_adj * (bld_acute_deaths_per_product * bld_survivor_life_share + bld_chronic_deaths_per_product * bld_dependent_survivor_life_share) * bld_value_per_death + trn_deaths_averted * trn_value_per_death * trn_survivor_life_share) / deaths_averted
rows.explainer: The death-weighted value across the branches, each death at its own age mix times its survivors' remaining-life share (acute bleeding, transfusion-dependent, cardiac arrest), so uov_deaths = deaths_averted × value_per_death as in the template.

rows.label: Units of value from deaths averted
rows.explainer: Deaths averted at their death-weighted value (value_per_death).

rows.label: Units of value from stillbirths averted
rows.explainer: A stillbirth averted at the site's one value (@givewell_shared.uov_per_stillbirth, GiveWell's), times your multiplier on the value of a life.

rows.label: Units of value from later-life income
Units of value from illness averted
rows.explainer: A share of the deaths' and income's value, the base GiveWell's supplementary share has.

rows.label: Share of blood products given for chronic and medical use
rows.explainer: The products not given for acute bleeding: haematology-oncology support (counted as deaths of transfusion-dependent patients below) and chronic anaemia (cancer, blood disorders, kidney disease).

rows.label: Of the products for chronic use, share going to patients whose survival over the year depends on transfusion
rows.explainer: Haematology and oncology patients through chemotherapy and stem-cell transplant, severe aplastic anaemia, thalassaemia major and sickle-cell crises: without platelet and red-cell support their treatment can't be given and many would die. Reference: of the 14.4 million components transfused in the US in 2023 (10.3 million red cells, 2.2 million platelets, 1.9 million plasma: McDavid et al. 2025, Transfusion, NBCUS 2023), platelets, about 15%, go mostly to haematology-oncology patients, who also take a large share of medical red-cell use. So about 40% of the non-acute products (about a quarter of all), from 20 to 60%. No US survey splits use by diagnosis.

rows.label: Risk a transfusion-dependent patient would die within the year without blood
rows.explainer: The share of a year's transfusion-dependent patients whose death a year without blood would bring forward, and that later years' products don't also claim: most dependent use is one-off chemotherapy or transplant episodes, and lifelong-dependent patients' (thalassaemia, myelodysplasia) later years are credited only to later products. Without transfusion intensive chemotherapy and transplant can't go ahead and severe aplastic anaemia is often fatal within months; but many would get less intensive treatment or fewer transfusions. About 30%, from 10 to 50%.

rows.label: Blood products a transfusion-dependent patient gets in a year
rows.explainer: A leukaemia induction or a stem-cell transplant takes tens of red-cell and platelet units; a thalassaemia patient gets one to two red-cell units every three to four weeks (15-25 a year). About 30, from 15 to 60.

rows.label: Deaths of transfusion-dependent patients averted per product (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Products for chronic use × the dependent share × their risk without blood ÷ products per patient-year: each product's share of a dependent patient's survival over the year.

rows.label: Weeks of anaemia relieved per product given for chronic anaemia
rows.explainer: A red-cell unit raises haemoglobin by about 1 g/dL, lasting a few weeks before the next transfusion; platelets prevent bleeding for days.

rows.label: Illness averted per blood product, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Products for chronic anaemia not counted as deaths above × the gain from severe to moderate anaemia (GBD 2019 disability weights) × the weeks relieved.

rows.label: Illness averted, in DALYs
Illness averted, in units of value
rows.explainer: The bridge from DALYs into units of value: the unit's conversion cancels it, so illness counts as healthy years whatever "Healthy year vs doubled-income year" is set to.

rows.label: Total units of value
rows.explainer: Illness and the other supplementary shares add to the modelled value side by side, as one sum of shares does in GiveWell's sheets; illness counted in DALYs comes in through its bridge.

rows.label: Units of value per dollar
Salaries and benefits in Biomedical and Training Services, FY2025 (US$)

source.title: The American National Red Cross, Consolidated Financial Statements, June 30, 2025 (audited by KPMG)
source.page: p. 5, Consolidated Statement of Functional Expenses (salaries, wages and benefits subtotal, in thousands; Biomedical 1,156,315 + Training 83,087)

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: The charity's own share from its audited functional expenses (about 55%).

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: The shared pay gap for health workers and field staff at nonprofits: phlebotomists, lab staff and instructors.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid by cash donations
Units of value per dollar you give
rows.explainer: The result per dollar, for the share of the full cost that cash donations pay (here: per dollar spent; donations fund none of it, so it has weight 0 in the charity's mix).

output.label: Units of value per dollar you give
